opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, we looked at it pretty seriously early on, because it's the most obvious path. When you have a team that's very good at physical simulation and high-performance computing, people come to you with problems: "Can you simulate this fluid for our product?" or "Can you build a solver for this engineering case?" And there's real money in that. Customers are willing to pay, and the work is technically interesting.

But when we thought it through, I felt it wasn't the right core business for us. Contract simulation work is essentially a services business. Every project is a bit different, so you're constantly customizing, and your revenue scales roughly linearly with headcount. If you want to double revenue, you more or less need to double the number of engineers. That's a fine business, but it's not what you build a technology company around if your goal is to make a tool that changes how many people work.

There's also an opportunity cost issue. Our best people are a scarce resource. If they spend all their time on one-off customer projects, they're not improving the underlying platform: the compiler, the language, the developer experience. And the platform is where the long-term leverage is. A good tool can serve thousands or millions of users without us being in the loop for each one.

So my view was that some project work can be useful, especially early on. It keeps you close to real problems, shows you what users actually need, and can help with cash flow. But it should serve the product, not replace it. The question we kept asking was: does this project make our core technology better for everyone, or does it just solve one customer's problem? If it's only the latter, we should be careful about taking it on.

In the end, I think the lesson is that you have to be honest about what kind of company you want to be. Services can look attractive because the revenue comes quickly, but it can quietly pull you away from building something that scales.

r002.rationale: It calls contract simulation a services business and says it was not the right core business, but does not assess its viability as a B2B business in China.

r003.rationale: The response discusses building a scalable platform, but does not attribute this choice to Hu’s personality or limit his focus to standardized consumer-facing products.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was something we looked at pretty early and decided against fairly quickly. When you build a simulation engine like Taichi, the obvious first revenue path is contract work: a studio or a manufacturer comes to you, says "we need a fluid sim for this scene" or "simulate this material under these conditions," and you deliver it. The demand is real, and the money is real.

But when I actually ran the numbers and thought about what the company would look like in three or five years, it didn't hold up. Contract simulation scales linearly with people. Every project needs an engineer, often a very senior one, sitting with the client, tuning parameters, debugging their specific setup. Your revenue grows exactly as fast as you can hire physicists who can also write production code, and those people are extremely rare. So you end up as a consulting shop with a nice engine, not a technology company.

The second issue is that each contract pulls the engineering team in a different direction. One client wants cloth, another wants granular materials, another wants real-time on a mobile GPU. All of that is interesting, but very little of it compounds. You finish the project, hand it over, and most of the learning stays in that one deliverable instead of in the product.

And the third thing was margins and ownership. Clients in simulation work usually want to own the output, sometimes even the custom code. So you're essentially selling your best engineers' hours at a fixed price, with limited ability to reuse what you built.

So the way we assessed it was: contract work is a fine bridge. It validates that people will pay, it tells you which problems actually hurt, and it keeps the lights on. But it's not the business. What we wanted was something where one improvement to the core technology benefits every user at once, where the open-source community does part of the exploration for us, and where we can productize the parts people keep asking for. That's a much harder path early on, because revenue comes later, but it's the only one where the company's value actually compounds.

r001.rationale: It names margins as an issue and explains that the company would sell engineers’ hours at a fixed price with limited reuse.

r002.rationale: It says contract work is not the business the company wanted, but does not mention China or assess its viability there as a B2B business.

r003.rationale: It does not connect the business choice to Yuanming Hu’s personality or to a preference for standardized consumer-facing products.

sol-6.1.text:
We considered doing simulation work on a contract basis because it was a straightforward way to generate revenue. A customer has a problem, we help them solve it, and they pay us. But the challenge is that each project can require a lot of custom engineering. When you finish one project, you have to find the next one, and growing the business means hiring more people to do that work.

So we saw it as a useful way to understand customers’ needs, but we wanted to build something more scalable: a product that many customers could use, where the engineering effort accumulates instead of starting over with every contract.

r003.rationale: The response favors a scalable product, but does not attribute that choice to Yuanming Hu’s personality or specify standardized consumer-facing products.
